explicit_validation.explanation: Paper explicitly compares LLM-as-a-judge (NLI model TRUE) with human evaluation on the same outputs from TTS ⊕ f. method, reporting Spearman and Pearson correlation coefficients between automatic and human judgments

prompts.notes: Prompt templates shown in Table in Appendix G (mentioned but not fully extracted in provided text), evaluation uses natural language inference (NLI) for entailment checking

inter_annotator_agreement.value: Exact match accuracy: 66.6%, Within-one accuracy: 84.9%, Mean absolute error: 0.56
inter_annotator_agreement.interpretation: Acceptable consistency with only minor scoring discrepancies

guidelines.notes: Full annotation guideline described in Appendix A, includes three qualitative evaluation metrics (Completeness, Conciseness, Traceability) on 5-point Likert scale

sample_size.notes: Validation conducted on randomly sampled 10 abstracts from test set, involving comparison of automatic vs human evaluation of claim recall

validation_results.summary_finding: LLM-as-a-judge shows moderate-positive correlation with human judgments (TRUE: ρ=0.612, r=0.577; GPT-4o performs best with ρ=0.80, r=0.77), indicating reasonable alignment but room for improvement

criteria_mapping.notes: LLM evaluation focuses on entailment-based metrics (claim recall/precision), while human evaluation uses qualitative 5-point Likert scales covering completeness, conciseness, and traceability
